newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Market, analysts welcome new Winterthur CEO.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Market, analysts welcome new Winterthur CEO.

text.p: Winterthur Insurance, Europe's fourth biggest insurer, on Wednesday named 42-year-old McKinsey consultant Thomas Wellauer as new chief executive in a strategic move greeted warmly by the stock market and analysts.

Wellauer will succeed Peter Spaelti, who announced earlier he would step down at the end of 1997 after almost 15 years as CEO to concentrate on his other post as chairman of the board, which he has held simultaneously since 1989.

Analysts said Wellauer's background as head of the Swiss financial unit at McKinsey's Zurich office meant he could expand on Winterthur's first steps into the growing international field of alliances between insurers and banks.
"It's good news for Winterthur...Wellauer knows the financial industry in general very well, not only insurers but also banks," said analyst Heinrich-Horst Wiemer from CS First Boston in Zurich.
Winterthur shares opened 17 Swiss francs higher at 1,018 francs after the early morning news and leapt five percent to an all-time high of 1,053 before easing a bit to around 1,050 in the afternoon.
Traders said Wallauer's appointment was good news because of his ties with former McKinsey associate Lukas Muehlemann, chief executive at banking major Credit Suisse Group.

On the one hand, Muehlemann's success at boosting earning power at his former company, reinsurer Swiss Re, and more than doubling its share price in two years after his start there in 1994 raised hopes that Wallauer would do the same at Winterthur.

Another point mentioned by traders was speculation that Wallauer's reign would lead to an even closer alliance between Winterthur and Credit Suisse, which agreed in late 1995 to cooperate in developing and selling financial products together with Swiss Re.

Winterthur, whose 1995 gross premiums rose nine percent to 22.3 billion Swiss francs, provides non-life and life insurance with its biggest market in Europe, led by Switzerland and Germany, as well as activities in North America and East Asia.

"For an internationally active company like Winterthur, which only has a third of its business in Switzerland, it is good to have somebody who comes from outside and knows the sector internationally, not just at home," said analyst Beat Alpiger at Bank Baer in Zurich.

Winterthur itself said Wellauer was well acquainted with the insurer through his work since joining McKinsey in 1986, including heading a number of projects helping multinational clients set strategy and reorganise.

"Since 1992, he has been involved in many of Winterthur's important strategic projects which means that he has already had an excellent insight into Winterthur and its organisation," a Winterthur statement said.

CS First Boston's Wiemer said one main challenge for Wellauer will be finishing a process of integrating Winterhur's widespread network of operations under a strategy launchyed in 1992 to clear up organisational lines and cut costs after a string o 1980s acquisitions.

"Just because you create a single legal entity does not mean the job is done. It means that everything is prepared for doing a good job....This will start having an effect in 1996 results (due May 14) and will continue in 1997 and 1998," Wiemer said.

Alpiger said he expected Wellauer to start demonstrating the bottom-line benefits of the cooperation with Credit Suisse and Swiss Re now that the first few products and joint ventures had been launched with a focus on Switzerland.

"Winterthur is only one-third active in Switzerland and Credit Suisse is a global player, so I would really expect cooperation not to be limited to little Switzerland but to extends abroad," Alpiger said.
